<reason>Both sides were strong and clash stayed narrow. A's organizing frame — every CON harm is someone reacting to a truth being revealed, so the cure is always fewer people knowing the fact — went essentially unanswered at the level of principle. B's best response was the decision-relevance standard (diner-menu fallacy: accurate numbers without cost context mislead) and the sharp paystub counter that the rider's price shows a stranger's willingness to pay, not the driver's wage. But B's core mechanism — drivers rejecting profitable trips out of insult — was met by A's informed-judgment turn, and B's behavioral cascade (cherry-picking, utilization collapse, cap politics) remained speculative, while A could point to functioning disclosed-split marketplaces. B's audits-only alternative conceded that the transacting parties should stay ignorant, which A exploited effectively in the closing. B executed well, answered pressure questions cleanly, and offered fresher original angles (cross-subsidy, tip-skipping perversity), but A controlled the terms of the debate and made the easier decision for a third-party reader. A's clipped opening is a minor execution cost.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A2.4's inversion — that drivers rejecting trips once the split is visible proves platforms were extracting value through information asymmetry — met its match in B2.4/B4.1's insistence that the rider's price adds nothing to dollars-per-hour math and only an insult cue. This exchange defined the debate; A's subsequent "managed ignorance" crystallization (A5.2) tipped it, since B's audits-and-averages answer left the two transacting parties as the only ones kept in the dark.</best_rebuttal>
